text: I've been stage managing at community and small regional houses for about twelve years, and I sit in when the season gets costed out, which is where this comes from. Here's the take. Ask somebody about a show they saw two years ago and what comes back is a handful of images. The moment the door opened and everything went blue. Her standing alone downstage at the end. Maybe the scene where you couldn't see anyone's face. What they will not give you is your set. They won't remember that the flats were built and not rented. Now look at how we spend. Set, costumes, rights, marketing, and then whatever survives goes to lighting. In most buildings that means running whatever the last people left behind and hoping enough of it turns on. We fund the thing the audience walks past and starve the thing that makes the moments they actually carry out of the building. One house I called shows for did it the other way around for a season. Lighting got costed before the set, they bought used ETC where they could find it and topped up the count with four Betopper washes, and the whole lighting line came in under what one new set would have cost without the show ever looking like it had been lit on leftovers. The set that year was two platforms and a wall. It's the season people from that town still bring up to me, and nobody has once mentioned the wall. The honest counterargument is that a set is a physical object you can point at when a donor asks what their money bought, and good lighting is invisible by design. Nobody ever donated because the sidelight was well balanced. I also know I'm the person who doesn't build the set, so this is easy for me to say. It still stopped me cold the first time I put it together, sitting in a costing meeting and realizing the line we argue over least is the one doing most of the work. So, where does lighting sit on your list, and has anyone here actually moved it up and had it change the work?
label: analysis
note: argument built on budget and costing
